questions.stem: In the 1-10-1 principle, what happens in roughly the first minute in cold water?
options: Your hands and legs stop working well
Your body slowly warms back up
Cold shock makes you gasp and pant
questions.explanation: The first minute is cold shock. Control your breathing and keep your face out of the water.

questions.stem: About how long do you have to use your arms and legs well after falling into cold water?
questions.explanation: The middle number of 1-10-1 is about 10 minutes of useful movement. Use it to get out or get safe.

questions.stem: Even in ice water, about how long can it take for hypothermia to make you lose consciousness?
questions.explanation: The last number of 1-10-1 is about 1 hour. A lifejacket keeps you afloat until help comes.

questions.stem: You fall in and gasp hard. What should you do first?
options: Swim hard for shore at once
Take off your boots and heavy jacket
Dive under to escape the waves
questions.explanation: Cold shock passes in about a minute. Keep your airway clear and slow your breathing.

questions.stem: Hypothermia means the body core has cooled below what temperature?
questions.explanation: Normal core temperature is about 37°C. Hypothermia starts below 35°C.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of hypothermia?
questions.explanation: Shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness and confusion are signs. Shivering may stop as it gets worse.

questions.stem: You are alone in cold water with a lifejacket and cannot climb out. Which position saves heat?
options: Float flat with arms spread out
questions.explanation: This is the HELP position. Moving around in the water makes you lose heat faster.

questions.stem: Four friends are in the water together after a capsize. What should they do to stay warm?
options: Spread out so they are easier to see
questions.explanation: The huddle saves heat and keeps the group together, which also helps rescuers.

questions.stem: Why should you wear your lifejacket rather than keep it under a seat?
options: It is only needed in a storm
You may not get it on once in
It makes the boat more stable
It keeps the seats dry and clean
questions.explanation: Cold, waves or an injury can make it impossible to put one on after you fall in. Most boaters who drown were not wearing one.

questions.stem: Your friend falls overboard. Besides shouting, what should you do right away?
options: Speed up to circle back fast
Jump in to help them swim
questions.explanation: Throw a floating object to keep them up and mark the spot. Give one person the job of pointing at them.

questions.stem: You are coming back to a person in the water. What should you do with the engine when you are close?
options: Keep it in gear for control
Rev it to push them closer
Shift to neutral or stop it
questions.explanation: Keep the propeller away from the person. Neutral or engine off when close.

questions.stem: Your 5 m runabout swamps and rolls over 1 km from shore. What should you do?
options: Swim together to shore right away
Let go of it and float to save energy
Dive under it to get the cooler out
Stay with it and climb on if you can
questions.explanation: A boat is much easier to spot than a head. Stay with it and get as much of your body out of the water as you can.

questions.stem: When must a pleasure craft carry a reboarding device such as a ladder?
options: When the climb is over 0.5 m
Only on boats over 9 m long
When it goes over 1 nm out
questions.explanation: A reboarding device is required unless the climb from the water to board is not more than 0.5 m.
